doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Listening habits and what makes a rhythm section swing
summary: He listens in the car and to the rhythm section alone, says swing is about emotion, and judges the whole production including engineering and artwork.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Do you ever multi-task when you’re listening? Even making coffee or oh I’ve got to go get the mail and the music’s playing, or do you sit and just totally concentrate on the selection?

I’ll do that in the car. I like to do that in the car, which is why I bought this car off lease because it still has a CD player. But that’s also part of the method of the madness you know. I’ll listen to it here and then I’ll say you know what? I want to take it for a ride. I’ll listen to it in a lot of different ways. I’ll listen to a track and only listen to the rhythm section, you know, foregoing the front line.

I had a question about that, I’m glad you said that. If you did a review on a record and let’s say it was sort of in — well here we go with labels — but mainstream I guess, and you were struck by how swinging the rhythm section is, for you, what makes that work? What makes that rhythm section swing more than some other ones?

I think that swinging in that particular instance is something that derives an emotional and rhythmic response from me the listener. Okay? One can talk about before the beat, on the beat, behind the beat, you know all that technological stuff, but it’s all about emotion. So quite honestly it’ll be rare — at least in my experience — where the rhythm section is really swinging and the vocalist or the front line is let’s say a little bit less energetic. Okay? You know you have to look at a production in its totality, meaning the front line, the rhythm section, the engineering. I also like to listen to these albums — or tracks — from a production standpoint. Okay? And having done a little bit of that with like Keith Fiala for example, as a matter of fact I have done a lot with Keith on a number of his singles and albums, you learn a little bit more. I mean I know nothing about, you know, sliding and equalizers and phasers and all of that. All I know is what I can hear here and

you know what good balance is, and you know what good mixing is, and you appreciate the production elements and the production values of what goes into the artwork. You know it’s almost like, and there are samples of this, it’s almost like a beautiful classic painting that has a gaudy, gaudy frame. Okay? And it’s like well I’m interested in the Mona Lisa, I’m’ not interested in this you know, gilded peeing cherubs and whatever it happens to be. You know? So it really is an immersion. You know? You really immerse yourself into, you know, that’s why I get on the album review side a lot of albums to listen to. And you know I tend to be very selective about what I’ll listen to. Sometimes that’s not a positive because you’ll miss something or you won’t review an album that really, really is something unique and special.
